c1.story:
Every Indian bank sells the same thing. Money. It buys money from you as a deposit, rents it out to someone else as a loan, and pockets the difference. There is no secret molecule, no patent, no factory. So why does the market pay several times book value for one bank and barely book value for another that looks, on the surface, almost identical?

Because the raw material is not the same price for everyone. A large private bank like HDFC Bank or ICICI Bank sits on an ocean of current and savings accounts, money that companies and households leave lying around for convenience and on which the bank pays very little. A newer bank has to coax deposits in with fixed-deposit rates that are visibly higher. Same product on the shelf, very different cost of goods.

The three doors sort Indian banks by that one fact and the habits that come with it. The large private franchises have the cheapest, stickiest money and the discipline to lend it carefully, so they keep the most of what they earn. The PSU banks, State Bank of India, Bank of Baroda, Punjab National Bank, Canara, have an enormous reach into every taluka and a deposit base that rarely leaves, but they also carry the government's priorities on their books, and their history is written in corporate loans that went bad. The mid-size private and small finance banks are the challengers: they pay more for deposits, so they must lend to riskier, higher-yielding borrowers to make the maths work.

A bank is only as good as the cheapest rupee it can borrow and the worst borrower it lends to.

Notice what that means for your holding period. The first door compounds quietly. The second is a cycle trade: PSU bank stocks were among the market's best performers after 2021 as old bad loans were recovered, and they can halve just as fast when the next wave arrives. The third door is a bet on execution, and execution is precisely where Yes Bank in 2020 and IndusInd in 2025 came unstuck.
c1.read:
The tiles are the three doors. Read each from top to bottom, and spend the most time on the bar.

  • The name and the line under it describe where the money comes from and where it goes: cheap current and savings accounts for the leaders, sticky government-bank deposits for the PSUs, costlier deposits chasing higher-yield loans for the challengers.
  • The tickers are the listed names that sit mostly behind each door. Click one to open its stock page. Mid-size names like IDFC First and AU Small Finance sit in the third tile even though they are growing fast; growth is not the same as a cheap deposit base.
  • The profit bar is the heart of the card. Large private banks sit at high, because cheap deposits and low bad loans let them keep most of the spread. PSU banks sit at medium: the spread is fine, but policy lending and the bad-loan cycle take their cut. Mid-size banks sit at low, because their deposits cost more and their borrowers default more.
  • The bet line tells you what you are really underwriting when you buy: steady compounding, a credit-cycle recovery, or a catch-up story that must avoid an accident.

Below the tiles, the analogy and so-what give you the one question to ask of any bank stock: what share of its money comes from current and savings accounts? Look that up in the latest investor presentation before anything else. It decides which tile a bank really belongs in, whatever it calls itself.

c2.story:
Picture a bank as a kitchen with five stations, except the ingredient going in and the dish coming out are both money. The trick is in what happens to it in between.

At the first station, money walks in through the front door: your salary sitting in a savings account, a company's float in a current account, a retiree's fixed deposit, and when that is not enough, bonds or borrowing from the RBI. This is where the cost of the raw material is set, and it is set mostly by habit. People do not shop for a savings account every week.

At the second station, a credit officer decides who gets that money and at what price. This is the most important job in the building and the one that is easiest to do badly in good times. The PSU banks' infrastructure lending of the boom years was decided here, and so was the cleaner retail book that let the private leaders sail through Covid.

The third station is the treasury, the quiet back room. By law a bank must park a slice of deposits in government bonds and another slice with the RBI as cash reserve. The treasury manages that pile and the mismatch between deposits that can leave tomorrow and home loans that run for twenty years. When bond yields move, this station books gains or losses before anyone notices.

The fourth station is payments and fees: cards, UPI, cash management, selling mutual funds and insurance to customers who already trust you. And the last station is the one nobody likes to talk about, collections and recovery: chasing late payers, restructuring, selling bad loans to asset reconstruction companies, and, since 2016, taking defaulters to the insolvency tribunal. Bhushan Steel and Essar Steel were resolved here and returned real money to the banks.

So where does competition come from, if not a foreign bank? From the edges. Mutual funds compete at station one. NBFCs and fintech lenders compete at station two. PhonePe, Google Pay and Paytm compete at station four.
c2.read:
Read the top row left to right: money comes in at the first box and goes out, hopefully, through the second, with the treasury, the fee business and the recovery desk following behind.

  • Each box names the station, what happens there and who stands there. Notice that the same names, HDFCBANK, SBIN, ICICIBANK, appear in the first two boxes. Banks are integrated: they own the deposit and the loan, which is the whole point of a banking licence.
  • The band row underneath shows who holds each station. The first three cells are coloured as Indian listed banks: deposits, lending and treasury all belong to them, with the RBI sharing the treasury cell because it sets the rules there. The last two cells are not coloured, because the fee station is shared with fintechs and the payments body, and recovery runs through courts and asset reconstruction companies the banks do not control.
  • There is no rival row, because no foreign bank stands anywhere meaningful in this kitchen. The note below the diagram tells you who the real rivals are: mutual funds for deposits, NBFCs and fintechs for loans.

Use the diagram to place news. A surge in SIP flows is a station-one story: deposits get dearer. An RBI tweak to risk weights is station two. A bond rally is station three, and shows up as treasury gains the same quarter. A tribunal resolution is station five, and arrives as a write-back of provisions. The so-what line is the key one: station one getting more expensive squeezes the margin even before a single loan goes bad.

c3.story:
A bank's customers are not one crowd. They are seven very different groups who happen to queue at the same branch, and each one brings its own risk and its own reward.

Start with the home buyer. A mortgage is the largest retail loan book in the country, and it is the gentlest: the borrower lives in the collateral, so defaults are rare and losses on default are small. The catch is that home loans are a fight on price. Every bank wants them, so the margin is thin.

Then the consumer: credit cards, personal loans, car and two-wheeler loans. This is where yields are fattest and where trouble starts first. When the RBI raised risk weights on unsecured loans in November 2023, it was telling banks, politely, that it thought this book was growing too fast. By 2024 card and personal-loan stress was showing up in results, exactly as the regulator had feared.

Small businesses borrow working capital and term loans and move with GST collections and local demand; they pay well and default in clusters when demand dips. Large corporates are the opposite: they borrow at the finest rates and, crucially, can skip the bank and go to the bond market when it is cheaper. The power, steel and telecom lending of the late 2000s came from this tile, and it wrecked PSU balance sheets for most of the following decade.

Farmers take crop and gold loans at subsidised rates and move with the monsoon and, occasionally, with a state election promising a loan waiver. The government and its companies borrow for infrastructure and absorb bonds. And then there is the group that is both customer and supplier: savers. They buy safety and convenience, and lately they have been comparing a fixed deposit with a mutual fund SIP on their phone.

A bank's loan mix is its personality. Tell me who it lends to and I will tell you how it fails.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read every tile in three lines.

  • The name is who is borrowing, or in the last tile, who is depositing.
  • The second line is what they take from the bank: mortgages, cards, working capital, term loans, crop loans, safety.
  • The third line is what moves them, and that is your watch list outside banking: rates, property prices, jobs, GST collections, the capex cycle, the monsoon, the budget, and the returns on competing investments.

A useful way to read the grid is to rank the tiles by yield and risk together. Consumers and small businesses sit at the top of both: the highest rates, the highest defaults. Home buyers and large corporates sit at the bottom: thin spreads, few defaults, though corporates default big when they do. Farmers and government sit outside the market logic, because policy sets their terms.

Then cross-check with card one. The large private banks lend across most tiles and fund it from the last one cheaply. PSU banks are heavier on corporates, farmers and government. Mid-size and small finance banks lean on consumers, vehicles, small businesses and microfinance, which is why their profit bar is low and their risk is high. The so-what line puts it in one sentence: the mix of borrowers is the risk profile, so read a bank's loan-book breakdown before its profit.

The savers tile is the odd one out and worth a second look. When its third line, deposit rates against fund returns, turns against banks, every other tile gets more expensive to serve.

c4.story:
Here is the thing that confuses every newcomer to bank accounts: the biggest expense is interest. In a cement company, interest is a financing cost buried near the bottom. In a bank, it is the raw material. The bank buys money and sells money, and interest paid on deposits is what the money cost.

So the first number to understand is the net interest margin, interest earned minus interest paid, divided by the assets that earned it. It is the spread, and it moves with two things: what the bank pays for deposits and what it charges on loans. The cruel part is timing. Since 2019 most retail floating-rate loans are linked to an external benchmark, usually the repo rate, so when the RBI cuts, loan rates fall almost immediately. Deposit rates, especially on fixed deposits locked in for a year or more, fall only as those deposits mature. That is exactly what happened in 2025: the RBI cut rates and reserve requirements, loan yields dropped first, and margins compressed for several quarters until deposit costs caught up.

Then come provisions, the money set aside for loans that will not come back. In a good year this line is small and nobody looks at it. In a bust it eats everything. Between 2015 and 2018, provisions turned several PSU banks' profits into multi-year losses, and the government had to put in fresh capital to keep them alive.

Capital is the line that ties it together. Every rupee lent needs a slice of shareholders' equity behind it, under the Basel rules. A bank that grows faster than it earns runs out of capital and must issue shares, diluting you. That is why a bank's return on equity and its growth rate must be read side by side.

In a bank, the margin decides the good years and the provisions decide whether there are any.

Fees from cards, wealth and insurance distribution are the cushion. They do not make a bank, but they smooth the years when the margin is squeezed.
c4.read:
The two charts walk a hundred rupees of bank revenue, mostly interest earned plus fees, down to what is left. Read left to right, and compare the two charts bar by bar.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is interest paid on deposits and borrowings, the raw material. For the large private banks it takes about half. For PSU banks it takes roughly six of every ten rupees. That gap is the cheap-deposit moat from card one, drawn in one bar.
  • The opex bar is staff, branches and technology. It is about the same bite in both charts, roughly a fifth. PSU banks have more branches and more staff, but a bigger book to spread them over.
  • The third bite is labelled depreciation and interest, but interest is already counted in the input bar. For a bank, read this bite as provisions for bad loans plus a sliver of depreciation. It is a little larger for PSU banks, which is their credit history showing.
  • The last bar is what is left. The private chart keeps a bit more than a fifth of revenue; the PSU chart keeps about a tenth. Same business, twice the profit per rupee.

These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes, not any bank's accounts. Hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below, the list of lines marks margin, provisions, deposit cost, interest and capital as clear yeses. Fee income is a sometimes. Working capital and capex get a no, because they are factory concepts; in a bank, liquidity rules and branch spending play those parts. If you open a bank's results with only five minutes, read the five yes lines in that order.

c5.story:
The Indian credit cycle runs on a roughly decade-long loop, and the last full turn is worth knowing by heart, because it explains why PSU bank stocks trade the way they do.

It began with optimism. From around 2009, banks, the PSU banks most of all, lent heavily to power plants, steel mills, roads and telecom. The economy was growing fast, every project looked viable, and lenders competed to fund them. Then the projects stalled: land could not be acquired, coal blocks were cancelled by the Supreme Court in 2014, approvals dragged. Instead of calling the loans bad, banks restructured them and waited.

The waiting ended in 2015, when the RBI under Raghuram Rajan launched its asset quality review and made banks recognise what everyone suspected. Bad loans at PSU banks climbed into the low teens as a share of loans. The RBI put the weakest under prompt corrective action, which in practice meant they could barely lend. The government then recapitalised the PSU banks and, in two rounds ending in April 2020, folded many of them into fewer, larger banks. The new insolvency code began returning money from big defaulters.

And then came the surprise. Covid was supposed to unleash a fresh wave of bad loans. It never came. From 2021 retail credit boomed, rising rates widened margins, and old written-off loans started coming back as recoveries. PSU banks posted record profits.

The cycle since has been gentler: deposits failed to keep pace with loans in 2024, the RBI leaned against unsecured lending, and the 2025 rate cuts squeezed margins. Now those margins look like they are bottoming, with balance sheets cleaner than at any point in a generation.

Bank stocks do not peak when profits peak. They peak when lending is easiest, which is when the next bust is being written.
c5.read:
The card has three parts: the clock, the timeline and the four hands. Read them in that order.

The clock splits the cycle into four arcs, boom, peak, bust and bottom, clockwise from the top. The years on each arc are the last full credit cycle: the infrastructure lending boom of 2009 to 2012, the stalled-project peak of 2013 and 2014, the recognition bust of 2015 to 2018, and the recapitalisation and merger bottom of 2019 and 2020. The arrow sits just short of the top, at the end of the bottom arc and about to cross into boom: early up, after a margin dip. Hover an arc to read what defined it.

The timeline runs from 2019 to now. The colours give the tone: two bust years for the shadow-bank freeze and Covid, a boom stretch for 2021 to 2023, a neutral peak in 2024, a bust-coloured 2025 for the margin squeeze and the IndusInd shock, and 2026 marked as now. Notice that the timeline is a shorter, sharper cycle than the clock, a margin cycle sitting inside the larger credit cycle.

The four hands are what you watch to move the arrow yourself.

  • Loan growth versus deposit growth: converging, arrow up. A healthy bank grows both together.
  • Net interest margin: bottoming, arrow flat. This is the hand the whole call hangs on; when it turns up, the profit upturn has started.
  • Unsecured retail and microfinance stress: easing, arrow up.
  • Credit cost: normal and below average, a mixed arrow. Low is good, but low can only go one way, so watch its direction, not its level.

The so-what below tells you who benefits first from this position: the large deposit franchises, then PSU banks on valuation.

c6.story:
If you want to know how a bank will do next year, you could study its management for weeks. Or you could look at what the RBI did last month. To an unusual degree, Indian bank earnings are set in Mint Street.

Three dials carry the most weight. The first is the policy rate. It is two-faced, and the mechanism is worth understanding. When the RBI raises rates, loans linked to the repo reprice upward almost at once, while deposit costs follow slowly, so margins widen for a while. That is what happened in 2022 and 2023. But higher rates also slow loan demand and strain borrowers. Cuts do the reverse: margins compress first, growth recovers later.

The second is system liquidity, the amount of spare cash sloshing around the banking system, along with the cash reserve ratio. When liquidity is tight, banks fight each other for deposits and pay up for them. When the RBI injects liquidity or cuts the reserve requirement, as it did in 2025, every rupee freed from the reserve is a rupee the bank can lend, and the deposit war cools. The third is credit growth itself: more lending is more earnings, provided it is the right lending.

Then come the supporting dials. Government bond yields move the treasury book: a rise means mark-to-market losses on the bonds banks must hold. Industrial activity tells you whether corporate borrowers can repay. Inflation decides how much room the RBI has. The household shift into markets is the slow one: every year, more savings go into SIPs and stocks instead of deposits, and banks pay more to hold on to the rest.

Finally, two small dials. When the rupee falls and the RBI sells dollars to defend it, it drains rupee liquidity from the system as a side effect. And the PSU bank index is a sentiment gauge on divestment and asset quality, a dial that reflects the cycle more than it drives it.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps.

  • Dial: the outside force.
  • Channel: how it reaches bank profits. For the policy rate, for example, the channel is that loan yields reprice fast and deposit costs slowly, which is why its effect is mixed.
  • A rise does: the effect of the dial going up. A green up arrow means a rise helps, a red down arrow means it hurts, and a diamond means it cuts both ways. Liquidity, credit growth, industrial activity and the PSU bank index are green. Bond yields, inflation, the savings shift and a weaker rupee are red. The policy rate is the diamond.
  • Weight: one to three dots. Three dots means the dial can make or break a year.

The last column shows today's reading where the dial maps to a series we track: the money market rate, our credit indicator, a government bond fund as a stand-in for yields, industrial output, consumer prices, the Nifty, the rupee and the PSU bank index. System liquidity has no live series, so it shows a dash; follow the RBI's daily liquidity operations in the news instead.

Scan the three-dot rows first: the policy rate, liquidity and credit growth. Then notice the odd one: the Nifty sits on the savings-shift row with a red arrow. A rising stock market is good for the economy, yet bad for deposit gathering, because it pulls savers away. The so-what tells you the minimum: track the policy rate and liquidity, one for the margin, the other for the cost of deposits.

c7.story:
Banks look like money machines on a good day. The bottlenecks explain why they are not valued like one, and why the gap between the best and the worst bank is so wide.

The first and newest bottleneck is the deposit itself. For decades, Indian households kept their savings in fixed deposits, gold and property. Since 2020 they have discovered mutual funds and the stock market in their millions. That money has not left the banking system entirely, but it now moves on its own terms, and banks have to pay more to keep it. When HDFC Bank merged with its parent HDFC in July 2023, it inherited a large loan book funded by borrowings rather than deposits, and spent the following two years slowing loan growth so deposits could catch up. Even the best franchise in the country had to wait for its raw material.

The second is the cycle of bad loans, which no regulation has ever abolished. It arrives about once a decade, and the last one cost PSU banks most of their profits for years. The third is government ownership: PSU banks are asked to lend to priority sectors, to hold rates when Delhi prefers, and to move at the pace of a ministry. That caps their returns and their valuations.

Then come the bottlenecks that move single stocks. Unsecured retail loans grew fastest and are now defaulting fastest. Governance lapses are the scariest: in March 2020 the RBI took over Yes Bank and wrote down its perpetual bonds, and in March 2025 IndusInd disclosed a gap in its derivative accounting that knocked roughly a quarter off its share price in a day and later cost its top two executives their jobs.

In a bank, a hidden problem is not a bad quarter. It is a question about every number the bank has ever published.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity label. The label tells you where the risk belongs in your thinking.

  • Structural rows are permanent and belong in your valuation: deposit mobilisation and government ownership. They set the ceiling on returns for the sector and especially for PSU banks.
  • Cyclical is the bad-loan cycle. It is not always on, but when it arrives it dominates everything else on this page.
  • Recurring rows come back again and again: unsecured retail stress, where the RBI has twice tightened rules, and governance and accounting lapses, which are the single-stock blow-ups. These deserve a news alert per bank you own.
  • Slow is regulatory capital and new rules, like expected-loss provisioning and stricter liquidity norms. They raise the bar gradually and with long notice.
  • Two-sided is fintech and NBFC competition. It takes high-yield borrowers and the payments relationship away from banks, but banks also partner with fintechs and lend to NBFCs, so a strong NBFC sector is partly a bank customer.

Read the table top to bottom with the so-what line beside it. The first two rows, deposits and the bad-loan cycle, decide the long-run returns of the whole industry. The governance row decides which individual bank turns a bad week into a lost decade. If you own a mid-size bank, that is the row to keep rereading, because it is the one the market prices most violently.

c8.story:
No Indian industry is more regulated than banking, and in no other industry does a single regulator touch so many lines of the profit and loss statement. The RBI licenses banks, sets the policy rate, decides how much of every deposit must sit idle as cash reserve or in government bonds, sets the capital behind each type of loan, and can bar a bank from a business overnight. Ask Paytm Payments Bank, which the RBI effectively shut down in early 2024.

Take the cash reserve ratio and the statutory liquidity ratio. Every rupee locked in the cash reserve earns the bank nothing. So when the RBI cut the cash reserve ratio in stages through late 2025, it handed banks a pool of free funds to lend, a direct boost to margins at a time when rate cuts were squeezing them.

Risk weights work more quietly. In November 2023 the RBI raised the capital banks must hold against consumer loans and against their lending to NBFCs. It did not ban anything; it simply made fast unsecured growth more expensive. In 2025 it rolled part of that back. Same effect as a rate change, aimed at one product.

Two big changes are on the horizon. Expected credit loss provisioning, due from April 2027, will make banks provide for losses they expect rather than losses that have happened. That means a one-time hit to capital, then smoother credit costs. And revised liquidity norms assume digitally accessible deposits can run faster, a lesson from the speed of bank runs abroad, so banks must hold more liquid bonds.

Beyond the RBI sit the insolvency code, which decides how much banks recover from failed companies; the finance ministry, which owns PSU banks and decides their mergers and divestments; and deposit insurance, raised to five lakh rupees per depositor after the PMC Bank collapse in 2019.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule. Read across: who or what it is, what it does, why it matters to a shareholder, and its status.

  • Always rows are the permanent machinery: the RBI itself, Basel capital rules, the insolvency code and deposit insurance. They change rarely, but every bank's earnings pass through them.
  • Live rows are moving prices today. The reserve ratios, where the 2025 cuts freed money to lend. Risk weights on unsecured loans and NBFC lending, raised in 2023 and partly rolled back. And the Department of Financial Services, whose divestment and governance calls move PSU bank stocks, the IDBI sale being the current example.
  • New is the revised liquidity coverage norm, which nudges banks to hold more bonds and fewer loans.
  • Coming is expected credit loss provisioning. Mark the start date in your calendar: banks with thin provision buffers will need capital, banks that have been over-providing will barely notice.

The quickest way to use the table is to ask, for each live row, which direction it moved last: loosening rules help margins and growth, tightening rules hurt. Right now most live rows have been loosening, which is part of why the call is constructive.

Dated regulatory news for banks, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab. RBI circulars are the ones to read in full.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces boil down to one question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? For most industries, the answer is a story about suppliers and customers squeezing the middle. Banking has a twist, because the supplier is you.

Depositors supply a bank's raw material. Individually they have no power at all; nobody negotiates their savings rate. But collectively they can drift away, and since 2020 they have, towards mutual funds and stocks. So supplier power has quietly risen from very low to moderate, and it is higher for PSU and mid-size banks, which need to pay up for deposits, than for the large private franchises with their sticky current accounts.

Buyers, the borrowers, split in two. A large corporate is a powerful buyer: it can issue bonds or play one bank against another, and it does. A family with a twenty-year home loan is a weak one: switching is a paperwork nightmare, so most never bother. That averages out to moderate pressure for both kinds of bank.

Rivalry is where the doors differ most. Everybody wants the same good borrower and the same salaried depositor. The private leaders compete on service and speed; PSU banks often compete on price, which is the most expensive way to compete.

The best news is the entrant spoke. A full banking licence in India is rare. The RBI has granted only a handful of full licences in the last two decades, and building a deposit franchise from scratch takes a generation. That is a moat no fintech can buy.

A fintech can win your payments in a weekend. Winning your salary account takes years.

Substitutes are real, though: NBFCs, fintech lenders and bonds substitute for loans, and funds substitute for deposits.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches out along a spoke, the more pressure that force exerts, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: large private banks, and PSU plus mid-size banks together. The first thing to notice is how similar they are. Unlike chemicals or metals, banks share most of their forces, because they sell the same product under the same regulator.

The differences sit on two spokes. On rivalry, the PSU and mid-size shape reaches a little further, because they compete harder on price. On supplier, the gap is the same size: depositors cost them more to win and keep. Those two small bulges are the visual version of the profit-bar gap on card one.

Then look at the shortest spoke, which is the same for both: new entrants, scored at the low end. The banking licence is the industry's best protection. The other spokes, buyers and substitutes, sit at moderate for both shapes.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero, no pressure, to three, heavy pressure, with a one-line reason. Use it as a template, not a verdict. For a specific mid-size bank funded by bulk deposits, you might push the supplier spoke higher still. For a large private bank with a dominant salary-account franchise, you might pull it in. The so-what line says where the profit ends up: with the cheapest deposits and the cleanest underwriting.

c10.story:
A bank's results presentation can run to fifty slides of segment data, product growth and digital adoption. You can read eight numbers instead and know almost everything that matters, in the order that matters.

Start with the net interest margin, the spread. Then the CASA ratio, the share of deposits sitting in current and savings accounts, which is the cheapest money a bank can get. A falling CASA ratio is a rising cost of funds on the way. Then compare loan growth with deposit growth: if loans are running well ahead, the bank is funding itself with dearer money or running down its liquidity, and either way the margin will feel it.

Next, the credit numbers, and here the trick is to read them as stock and flow. Gross and net bad loans, or NPAs, are the stock: the pile of loans already gone bad. The slippage ratio is the flow: fresh loans turning bad this quarter. A bank can show a falling stock simply by writing off old loans while the flow quietly rises. Credit cost, provisions as a share of loans, tells you what the bad loans are costing this year.

Finally, the outcome and the cushion. Return on assets is profit per rupee of balance sheet, the cleanest single measure of a bank's quality, because it is not flattered by leverage. And the core equity capital ratio tells you how much room the bank has to grow before it needs to ask you for more money.

Watch slippages, not NPAs. The pile tells you where a bank has been; the flow tells you where it is going.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question each number answers. Read the rows in order and you go from spread, to funding, to credit quality, to profit, to capital.
  • What good looks like is the only column on the page with figures, and it usually gives two benchmarks: one for the large private banks and a lower one for PSU banks. That split matters. A PSU bank at the PSU benchmark is doing fine; holding it to the private standard will make every PSU bank look broken.
  • Today's industry median shows a dash on every row for banks. That is not missing data in the sense of a bug: our medians come from standard company filings, which carry no margin, CASA or NPA lines. For banks, these numbers live in the quarterly investor presentation and the RBI's own data.

So use the table as a checklist rather than a scoreboard. For each bank you own, fill in the eight numbers from its latest presentation and set them against the good column. Then pay special attention to three pairs: margin with CASA, because cheap deposits protect the spread; loan growth with deposit growth, because the gap is borrowed profit; and NPAs with slippages, because the flow leads the stock. A bank that passes all three pairs is rare, and usually expensive for a reason.

c11.story:
The good news about banks is that the industry tells on itself early. Much of what will be in next quarter's results is already published somewhere before the quarter ends.

The RBI releases system-wide loan and deposit growth every fortnight. That is the same-quarter read: you can see the gap between loans and deposits narrowing or widening long before any bank reports. Government bond yields hit treasury books the same quarter too.

One quarter out, the RBI's policy decisions and liquidity operations start flowing through to margins: loans reprice within the quarter, deposits over several. Mutual fund SIP inflows tell you how hard deposit gathering will be. GST collections and industrial output tell you about the health of small businesses and corporates. Microfinance collection efficiency, the share of dues actually collected, warns about bad loans at small finance banks.

Furthest ahead are the credit bureau reports. When late payments on cards and personal loans start creeping up in bureau data, the slippages arrive about two quarters later. That is how the unsecured stress of 2024 was visible in bureau data well before it hit bank results.

Put it together and you get the rule. Banks are in a genuine up-cycle when three things hold: loan growth is healthy and funded by deposits, margins are steady or rising, and credit cost is low and stable. Right now two of the three are ticking. The missing one is the margin, still bottoming after the rate cuts. That is why the call reads early recovery: the hard part, clean balance sheets and a funded book, is done, and the profit upturn is waiting for the margin to turn.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to read the channel through which it reaches bank earnings.

  • Far left, same quarter: the fortnightly RBI credit and deposit data, and government bond yields. These tell you what is happening now.
  • Middle, one quarter ahead: RBI policy and liquidity, SIP inflows, GST and industrial output, and microfinance collection efficiency.
  • Right, two quarters ahead: credit bureau delinquency reports, the earliest warning on the chart.

Use the chart as a reading order. Each quarter, look at the bureau data first, then the middle dots, then confirm with the fortnightly numbers.

Below the chart is the rule with its three signs. Loans funded by deposits: a tick, the gap has narrowed. Margins steady or rising: a cross, still bottoming after rate cuts. Credit cost low and stable: a tick, with unsecured stress easing. Two ticks out of three, and the rule's own wording tells you what the missing one costs: lose the margin and earnings stall; lose credit cost and the stocks fall. So today's cross is the milder kind.

The call box then gives the view, the three points behind it, and what would change it: another round of deep cuts before deposits reprice, rising unsecured or small-business slippages, or a sharp move of savings out of deposits. Treat those three as alerts. The second one would flip a tick to a cross, which is the expensive kind.
